simulating the same objects on opposite sides of the planet. And in some cases, it's important that
these things stay in sync, and in some it may not be. Could you maybe give some examples of cases

because real-time strategy games, there may be hundreds of different units that need to be
simulated. And if you have to simulate all these characters on the server, that could be a heavy

distinctly remember both Half-Life 2 and Crayon Physics. Crayon Physics, you had a kind of canvas
and a challenge to get one object from A to B through whatever means necessary. And you could draw

to it. But actually, mathematically, in some sense, it may be the simplest shape. That's correct.
When you collide two spheres in a physics engine in 3D, you just need to compute the distance
between the two center points and then discount the radiuses of the two spheres. And then that gives
you the distance between those spheres. So it is very simple to do those calculations. It's probably
one of the simplest collision algorithms you can have in a physics engine. Whereas doing the same

computationally, it gets quite hairy quite quickly. Yes, you can actually think of it in terms of

radius. A capsule needs two points and a radius. A box needs eight points. The radius is zero. A

of points involved. I see. So if an object in the game's world can be assembled from primitive
shapes like circles and capsules, as opposed to being what we might picture as a polygonal model, it

to what I was talking about earlier, where when we're developing a game, we get to determine the
content. We get to determine the abstractions that we're going to make in the physical
representation of the world. So when I'm making a crate, I would just make it as a box rather than
giving it a detailed mesh with thousands of triangles, because that is just going to have much
better performance characteristics. I see. I see. And again, on the subject of performance, these
days, often developers are increasingly looking to shift work from the CPU to the GPU. Is that also
true of physics engines in games? That is often something that is very interesting to look at, and

Yeah. So multithreading is very important for a physics engine. Ideally, we want to scale linearly
with the number of cores. Generally, that's not completely feasible in a physics engine because
there are always going to be some serial aspects. The challenge is to reduce those serial aspects as
much as possible. So a lot of effort in the multithreading design for physics engine is about

contact points, as I mentioned, the collision between shapes is quadratic in the number of points.
So what we can do with SIMD is we can take some of that work and have that work be done in groups of

between those two boxes to see if they're colliding or not. So if you think about that, every edge
pair is quadratic. So what you can do is you can group up four edge pairs and then use SIMD

instructions are called SIMD because it's a single instruction that takes multiple data. So that is

able to add two numbers together. SIMD allows you to pack four numbers from one set together and
pack another four numbers and then add them all at the same time and read out the four results,
which is why you talk about solving multiple things together in lockstep in groups of four. Exactly.
So it could be with SSE2 or NEON, maybe doing groups of four. There's AVX2, which lets you do groups

advantages. First of all, I mentioned earlier that we can do offline computations and that they
should compare to the online, the real-time computations. So we could take an algorithm that we've
optimized and then compare that result with a brute force approach. So that's one thing that we can
do. And we can do that as a unit test. That's fairly straightforward to set up. Another thing that
we have to advantage is physics simulation is very visual. So I always create some sort of visual
representation of the simulation so that I can study it and make sure it looks right. I will add all

two tools that we have working for us. I suppose manual testing is still something that's quite

independent of a game or independent of a game engine, then you can create an iterative environment
where you can test very rapidly changing algorithms, changing approximations, changing your data
format, optimizing things. And you can do that in a very focused way with a separate physics engine.
See, so speaking of physics engines as separate libraries from games, let's talk a bit about Box3D.
So you've recently released this engine. There's a really great introduction video you have on
YouTube, which we'll include in the show notes where you demonstrate a lot of the key features so
listeners can check that out. And I'd like to dig into your thinking a little bit behind some of the

the lessons in software design or architecture you're bringing into the new version, the 3D version
of this library? Yes. So Box2D started out as a tutorial for a conference. My goal was I want to
create a minimal set of code that shows how to stack boxes. That hard problem that we talked about,
which computationally is usually done in order and cubic time, which is not feasible. So Box2D
started out as about 200 lines of code that showed, here's how you can stack some boxes in linear

shared. And so I decided to make that an open source project. So this is the era where Crayon

And this was around 2006, 2007 that Box2D came out. And that was also the time of when the iPhone
came out. And then people were able to easily download games to their phone. And people found that
they could write games using physics to create a lot of engagement on that platform. So this really
was kind of a golden area of 2D game physics. That project evolved over time. And I used it as a

regular job. But on the side, I was developing this 2D technology. And so that evolved over the
years. It had starts and stops on and off. Around 2022, I decided I wanted to really see how far I

pedagogical. It was a learning platform for myself just to try new solver techniques, new
algorithms. It transitioned from being a C++ library to being a C library. It had multithreading. It

of them we may have mentioned already in terms of islands and sleeping objects and things like that.

earlier, finding all the pairs of objects that might be touching, that's done in parallel. The
narrow phase, finding all the contact points between the objects, that's done in parallel. And then
the big challenge for multithreading for game physics is the solver. We talked about islands as
being one potential way of multithreading the solver aspect. That can start to fall apart, though,
when you have very large islands. So I decided to take a different direction than using islands for
the solver aspect. What I do there is graph coloring. Graph coloring of the connections between the
shapes, so the contacts, the contact points. Those get colored according to what bodies they're
interacting with. And with this graph coloring technique, you can find, so say color one is red, and
then color two is green, and color three is blue. So now you've bucketed all of these constraints

color red, none of those are touching the same two bodies. So you can think of those as micro

first job of that system is to create a clone of the world as a single blob of data, essentially.

just basically doing mem copies of big arrays. So it's a plain old data. So that makes it fairly
straightforward. And then how it proceeds is I have that initial snapshot of the world. Then I
record all the inputs to the world. So if you applied a force to a body or you changed the friction
value of some material or you added or removed a body, all those events get recorded into the
stream. And then when you go to replay, what it will do, it will create a new physics world, load
that snapshot into it, and then as you're viewing that replay, it will replay those events that were
recorded. And it will actually do a live simulation there. To make that work, it relies on the
entire process being deterministic. I see. And can you give an example of a specific gameplay or
physics bug that this helped you to debug? Yes. So in our game, The Legend of California, we have
mining. And we've been working on improving the features of that system and making it feel more
visceral, more physical. So we have mining with voxels, but they're not Minecraft-style mining. It's
more these voxels are curved and we build meshes around them. So when you're mining, you will have a
pickaxe and you hit the wall with the pickaxe and then chunks will break off. So we started making
those chunks have a higher fidelity of shape, that they actually represent the pieces that are
removed. However, we were not quite happy with how the pieces moved when they became physical, when
they became rigid bodies. And it was hard to see in the game exactly why that was. There's a lot of
high movement speed. It's hard to visualize all the collision that's there. You're in a mine. It's
dark. The lighting's not maybe ideal. So I made a recording of that. And then I was that digging
process in the mine. I brought that into my replay viewer and then I was able to scrub time forward

they actually look like? What's their physical representation look like? Are they capsules? Are they
convex hulls? And when they spawn into the world, are they overlapped with the wall? Are they in
free space? And what is causing them to move the way that they're moving? And so with the system, I
was able to do this task in just a couple hours, which if I was trying to do this within the game
engine, it would have been much more difficult. Yeah, that sounds super powerful. And I know that
the game development community is very excited about Box 3D. And who knows, maybe it will promote a
generation of physics-based games in the same way that Box 2D did. Aaron, it's been really great
discussing video game physics with you. Are there any major areas we didn't cover which you'd like
to mention briefly before we wrap up? I think that's it. I'm very happy with the reception for Box
3D. And yes, part of my goal is to inspire people to make games with fun physics aspects. Amazing.
So lastly, if people want to follow you or they're interested in tinkering with Box 2D or Box 3D in
their own projects, where can they find out more? I recommend first head to Box2D.org. That also
covers Box 3D. And then I also have a YouTube channel that you can find using my name fairly easily.
And I like to post fun physics videos there. Awesome. Thanks again, Aaron, for the discussion. We'll
be sure to include those links and other useful resources in the show notes available at sc-
